meta.inputs_absent_note: These were named as inputs for an earlier stage but do not exist on disk: no stage wrote them. They are not needed: every other-works entry now has two to four independent reviews on disk.

rules.R1-R8 (other works, all reviewers count): APPROVED (quote corpus) only if EVERY reviewer who examined the entry says APPROVE for verbatim use and all agree on identity (same text source, or the same imprint year for different scans of one edition), rights tier (the same class, A1 or A2) and extraction path (an adapter all of them name); APPROVED-LINKOUT-ONLY if every reviewer says link-out only and all agree on identity, the recorded tier being the MORE restrictive one when they differ; REJECTED only if every reviewer rejects, each with evidence; any other disagreement, any request for human review and any REJECT against a non-REJECT is NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW with every rationale kept; fewer than two reviewers is NOT-VERIFIED
rules.R17 (guard): an APPROVED entry whose Internet Archive text source did not answer HTTP 200, or whose own metadata is dated after 1930, goes to a human
rules.R9-R13 (Official Records): APPROVED-CROSSWALK iff report number, author, side and first page agree with the OCR header index of the Internet Archive scan and no audit reviewer found the first page wrong; APPROVED-POINTER for Part XIII pages iff the page exists and its side label agrees; otherwise NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW. The description of an OR entry is marked untrusted when the audit sample shows the template is systemically inaccurate (95% Wilson lower bound of the not-accurate share above 10%)
rules.R14: DUPLICATE only on a hard identity (same HathiTrust volume id confirmed by the catalog API, or the same document id)
rules.R16: NOT-VERIFIED: nothing is approved on automated checks alone or on one reviewer

reviews.evidence: Scan p. 14 (IA 271 n31, viewed): No. 1 heading mid-page, after the previous report ends; rank, name, unit match the list. Halleck, General-in-Chief, writes "a summary of military operations since my last annual report"; four rows of "* * * * * * *" mark passages the OR omitted; the Gettysburg part is a few paragraphs (e.g. "Reynolds moved up to that place on July 1") and the only loss wording is "without serious loss on either side". pp. 14-21 also hold addenda (a Dec 15, 1863 letter from the Department of the East and a letter signed Geo. G. Meade to a general at Lookout Valley, Tenn.).

reviews.evidence: IA scan image n31 (viewed) is printed p. 14 and holds the end of the contents list (No. 354-378). Mid-page 'No. 1. Report of Maj. Gen. Henry W. Halleck, General-in-Chief, U. S. Army, including operations in Southeastern Virginia and West Virginia', dated 'Washington, D. C., November 15, 1863', 'a summary of military operations since my last annual report', then a row of asterisks. OCR text read in full: 'Reynolds moved up to that place on July 1', Meade took command June 28, a short account of July 1-3, and total Union loss 'Killed, 2,834; wounded, 13,709; missing, 6,643; total, 23,186' with the footnote 'But see revised statement, p. 187'. Four '* * * * * * *' rows mark passages the OR omits (pp. 14, 17, 17, 18). The report ends p. 18 with 'All of which is respectfully submitted. H. W. HALLECK'. Addenda Nos. 1-4 follow: Dix to Halleck (Dec 15, 1863, York River expedition), Halleck to Dix (Dec 20), Butterfield to Meade (Jan 23, 1864, Harper's Ferry), Meade to Butterfield (Feb 4, 1864). The p. 22 header precedes 'No. 2. Report of Brig. Gen. Hermann Haupt', so pp. 14-21 is exact. The contents-list line and the Civil War Cycling index (OR 27,1:14-21) match the title exactly. Hall: the brigade "had, on the morning of July 2, just completed a march of about 190 miles with scarcely a day's rest"; "The rebel General Barksdale was mortally wounded and two colors left on the ground"; printed as "Reports": a second letter to Col. Townsend lists flags the brigade captured. The first paper is signed Colonel, 7th Michigan, and 1st Lieut. 5th U.S. Artillery. Dixon note: list wording matches the double-asterisk mark in the Civil War Cycling index (fetched), which credits it to B. Y. Dixon's guide (not consulted).

reviews.evidence: IA scan image n452 (viewed) is printed p. 435. Top: end of Lt. Col. W. L. Curry's report (106th Pa). Lower half: 'No. 109. Reports of Col. Norman J. Hall, Seventh Michigan Infantry, commanding Third Brigade. Hdqrs. Third Brig., Second Div., Second Corps, Pleasant Valley, Md., July 17, 1863.' OCR text read for the first ~6.5k and last ~7.5k characters of 19.4k (middle not read): the brigade 'had, on the morning of July 2, just completed a march of about 190 miles with scarcely a day's rest'; 42nd NY and 19th Mass lost 'nearly one-third of their number'; 'The rebel General Barksdale was mortally wounded and two colors left on the ground'; 'Twenty battle-flags were captured in a space of 100 yards square'; 'about 150 men were killed or wounded' on July 2; Garnett and Armistead picked up. Signed 'NORMAN J. HALL, Colonel, Commanding Brigade' p. 441, then a second paper 'New York, August 3, 1863 ... Col. E. D. Townsend', naming the flags captured by 19th Mass, 42nd NY, 59th NY and 7th Mich men; ends p. 442. Printed heading and contents list both say 'Reports ... commanding Third Brigade'. Civil War Cycling index: OR 27,1:435-442 with a '**' Dixon flag (confirmed on that page; Dixon's book itself not seen). Listed links not opened (blocked).
reviews.extraction_notes: Text path: IA OCR djvu.txt or the historian adapter (or27-1:0109, 3,202 words, flagged composite). The heading is mid-page on p. 435. Two papers (report and the Aug 3 flags letter) need separate attribution and dates. Contains self-promoting claims ('turning point of the battle of July 3') and accusations of colors being 'stolen' that should be attributed as Hall's opinion. OCR noise: page number '43 1' for 437, minor glitches. Footnote 'Embodied in revised statement, p. 176' (casualties).

reviews.evidence: IA scan image n816 (viewed) is printed p. 799. Top: the daily march log at the end of Lt. Col. James C. Rogers's report (July 5-16). Lower part: 'No. 280. Report of Col. E. Livingston Price, One hundred and Forty-fifth New York Infantry. In the Field, Camp near Snickersville, Va., July 23, 1863', 'the services rendered by my command during the operations of this army, from July 1 to 15'. OCR read in full (pp. 799-802): 'my command moved from Littlestown, Pa., and halted about 2 miles from Gettysburg'; stone-wall line July 2, 'Company C ... lost 1 private killed and 2 wounded' on July 3; 'several of my men had been wounded by the fire of our own artillery' and the brigade colonel said 'not to fret'; then the pursuit to Fair Play, Williamsport and Pleasant Valley, 'over 150 miles'. Signed 'ED. LIVINGSTON PRICE, Colonel 145th New York Volunteers' p. 802 to 'Capt. E. J. Rice, A. A. A. G., First Brig., First Div., Twelfth A. C.', then No. 281. Civil War Cycling index: OR 27,1:799-802; contents list matches. Listed links not opened (blocked).

OCR noise: 'Snickers ville', 'Ya.', stray 'I' and '%' marks. The report covers July 1-15 (about 3/4 of it the battle days, the rest marches); the friendly-fire episode on July 3 is the most distinctive passage.

reviews.evidence: IA scan image n895 (viewed) is printed p. 878. The top two-thirds are the '[Inclosure.] Report of Casualties in batteries of the Artillery Reserve' table that belongs to Tyler's report No. 315. Below it, 'No. 316. Report of Lieut. Cornelius Gillett, First Connecticut Heavy Artillery, Ordnance Officer, Artillery Reserve. Camp near Warrenton Junction, Va., August 23, 1863. Captain: I have the honor to report that ... I proceeded with the ammunition train of the Artillery Reserve on July 2 from Taneytown to the position then held by our army near Gettysburg.' OCR read in full (pp. 878-879): the train was parked 'in a field to the right of the road' and supplied the batteries 'by General Hunt's direction'; about seventy teams sent to Westminster on July 3; at 2 p.m. 'Several shells passed over the train, and three or four fell among the teams, only one exploding', a mule killed; issue table 'Total issued at Gettysburg 19,189' rounds and '4,694 rounds' remaining; a recommendation against sending loaded wagons to batteries in action. Signed 'C. GILLETT, Second Lieutenant, and Ordnance Officer, Artillery Reserve' to Capt. C. H. Whittelsey; No. 317 follows on p. 879. The Civil War Cycling index (OR 27,1:878-879) matches and carries a '**' Dixon flag (not verified against Dixon's book). The contents-list line for No. 316 is blank in the OCR, but the heading is exact. Listed links not opened (blocked).
reviews.extraction_notes: Text path: IA OCR djvu.txt or the historian adapter (or27-1:0316, 539 words). Page 878 begins with Tyler's casualty table (inclosure to No. 315), so a page-level extraction must cut at the 'No. 316' heading. The ammunition-issue table is OCR-scrambled and one figure is lost (Hunt's lot of 360 rounds, inferred from the 19,189 total), so use the image n895/n896 for any numbers. A logistics report, so it is a source for ammunition supply and the July 3 cannonade effect on the trains, not for infantry or artillery combat.

Early's text states he reports 'the operations of this division during the recent campaign, commencing with its departure from Fredericksburg, and ending with its arrival in the vicinity of Orange Court-House'. The report is signed 'J. A. EARLY, Major-General, Commanding Division' on p. 473, to Maj. A. S. Pendleton. The casualty return (No. 471) starts on p. 474. Concrete content: 'On June 4, the division marched from Hamilton's Crossing'; Winchester loss 'slight, consisting of 30 killed, 143 wounded, and 3 missing'; 'My loss in the three days' fighting at Gettysburg was 158 killed, 796 wounded, and 227 missing'; Avery mortally wounded on Cemetery Hill July 2. pp. 459-473 match the entry and the CWC index, which marks this report with the Dixon asterisk (best overall reports on the battle). That attribution comes from CWC's index, not from Dixon's book.

rationale.evidence: Did not fetch the Perseus URL (robots.txt Disallow: /; per the brief). Found the article in the Internet Archive scan southernhistoric7187sout (SHSP Vol. VII, University of Florida; metadata, page map and djvu.txt 1,764,017 bytes fetched; item page .../page/401 returned HTTP 200). The contents list gives 'Report of General J. E. B. Stuart ... 401'; the printed heading is 'The Gettysburg Campaign - Full Report of General J. E. B. Stuart' at p. 401 and the running head 'Gettysburg Campaign - Report of General Stuart'; it ends before p. 435 ('Barbara Frietchie' refutation). Page map: p. 401 = leaf 413, p. 434 = leaf 446 (confidence 100, 590 of 608 leaves labelled). Claim 1, Aldie/Middleburg: the text has the passage on Fitz Lee's brigade moving 'towards Aldie via Middleburg' and 'At Aldie ensued one of the most sanguinary cavalry battles of the war'. Claim 2, ride around the army: the text says the indications 'favored my successful passage in rear of the enemy's army' and continues to Dranesville and Rowser's Ford. The editor's bracketed note says the Society had printed only a fragment of Stuart's report in August 1876 and was now, thanks to Maj. H. B. McClellan, giving the 'full text'. So 'reprinted by the Society' is wrong: this was the Society's first complete printing. I compared with the repo's OR27 Part 2 OCR (read-only): the OR text has the same body ('mobilized army', 'passage in rear of the enemy's army') but its salutation is 'General:' where SHSP addresses 'Colonel R. H. Chilton, Chief of Staff', and it capitalises 'southern' differently, so the two printings are variants.

rationale.evidence: The listed Perseus URL (doc=Perseus:text:2001.05.0120:chapter=9.72) was NOT fetched. I fetched www.perseus.tufts.edu/robots.txt (HTTP 200): the 'User-agent: *' block ends 'Disallow: /' with only /hopper/grants, research, about, collections and index.html allowed, and the /hopper/text allow line is commented out. I found the article independently through the IA advancedsearch API and read three scans: southernhistoricv7sout (Allen County PL, 608 images, OCR 1,759,239 bytes), the UF scan southernhistoric7187sout (610 images, 1,764,017 bytes) and the monthly issue sim_southern-historical-society-papers_1879-09_7_9 (Vol 7 Iss 9, 1879-09, 126,505 bytes). The title page reads 'Volume VII. January to December, 1879'; the contents list gives 'Report of General J. E. B. Stuart ... 401'. The p. 401 heading is 'The Gettysburg Campaign - Full Report of General J. E. B. Stuart' under 'Vol. VII. Richmond, Va., September, 1879. No. 9', identical to the entry title (my own read; all three OCRs agree). An editor's bracketed note says SHSP had printed only a fragment (Aug 1876) and now, through Major H. B. McClellan, gives 'the full text'. The report is headed 'Headquarters Cavalry Division, Army of Northern Virginia, August 20th, 1863. To Colonel R. H. Chilton' and runs pp. 401-434 (signature on p. 434, then list of inclosures A-E). Concrete checks: Aldie ('one of the most sanguinary cavalry battles of the war', p. 403) and Middleburg (pp. 402-408) are covered; so are the ride via Westminster and Hanover (pp. 412-414), Carlisle (pp. 414-415), Gettysburg July 2-3 (pp. 415-418) and the retreat to the Potomac and Shepherdstown (to p. 434). The 'Aldie, Middleburg and the ride' part is correct but incomplete. 'Reprinted' is not supported. The repo's own OCR of OR vol. 27 pt. 2 (historian-src/raw/or27/normalized-2.txt) opens the same Aug 20 report with a different salutation ('General:' and no addressee, 'on June 16' where SHSP has 'on the 16th day of June, 1863'), so the two printings differ in wording and I did not diff them further. The repo's OR index holds the report inside composite record or27-2:0565 (pp. 679-720), so the Historian already ingests this report from the OR. Circumstantial only: the article sits in issue No. 9 and the Perseus link says chapter=9.72, which is consistent but proves nothing.

Talcott': the printed contents list says p. 12, but the running head on p. 12 is 'Work of the Ordnance Bureau', and the article starts on printed p. 21 (leaf 33 in the Allen scan, leaf 39 in the UF scan) and ends p. 37. Dateline: New Oxford, Adams Co., Pa., 2 Oct 1863, addressed to Rood. Himes was at Carlisle for commencement about 25 June, saw citizen militia and two New York regiments man works a mile west, and left for home over the mountains as the rebels were reported in sight, i.e. before the occupation. The rest describes his own village under Gordon's brigade on Saturday (27 June), the 30 June cannonade at Hanover, his walk to Gettysburg on 1 July (after the Federals were driven through the town; Confederate pickets would not let him on the field), being turned out on the morning of 2 July, a report to Kilpatrick, and an enclosed fern from Round Top. Himes to Ogden N. Rood', 13 pages, Date October 2, 1863, Gift of Mary Himes Vale and Sarah Vale Rush, tags Battle of Gettysburg / Invasion of Carlisle / Invasion of Pennsylvania (no Shelling tag); its PDF link is archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/MC2000-1_b10_f10.pdf. That path has no capture; the same file under files_war/mc2000-01_b10_f10.pdf has two captures per CDX (20240225221947, 1,035,028 bytes; 20240703042213, 4,992,538 bytes). Read the typed text (OCR layer, noisy) and compared with the manuscript scans on sheet 1 and the last sheet: they agree (sheet 1 'preferring to look the Johnnies in the eye'; last sheet 'a piece of fern for Mrs Rood from Round Top ... I have a Rebel bone'). Content checks of the entry's description: he writes from New Oxford, says he was in Carlisle for Commencement about 25 June, describes the alarm, rifle pits dug about a mile west of town by the 'negro population', citizen soldiers supported by 'two N. York militia regts', then says he and his brother drove home over the mountain; he was NOT in Carlisle for the occupation (27-30 June) or the shelling (1 July). The rest covers Gordon's brigade passing through New Oxford on Saturday 27 June, the Hanover cavalry fight 30 June ('Stuart in person charged on Gen. Kilpatrick's column'), walking 17 miles to Gettysburg on 1 July 'just after the Rebs had driven our men through the town', being turned back by a Confederate officer, Kilpatrick's column passing on 2 July, and the Round Top fern. Hence 'Carlisle civilian ... occupation and shelling of the town' is wrong on three counts (not a Carlisle resident, no occupation, no shelling). Himes is the Dickinson alumnus and later professor (Dickinson current people page: 'Professor Charles F. Himes, ... Class of 1855', LL.D. 1896).

So the Confederate presence in the diary is at New Oxford, Hanover and the Gettysburg road, not in Carlisle, and nothing is said of the shelling.

In the volume's contents item XVIII is 'The 12th Alabama Infantry, C. S. A.; Its Organization, Associations, Engagements, Casualties, etc. By Robert E. Park, late Capt. Co. E., 12th Alabama, 193' (next item at 297). The editor's headnote (p. 193) says the piece 'consists of extracts from the War Diary of Robert Emory Park' with materials he collected; that the part of the diary for 1864-65 appeared in SHSP 1-3 (1876-77); and that the earlier part (January 1863 to January 1864, Chancellorsville, Gettysburg, the march into Pennsylvania) appeared in vol. The page <title> is empty. Heading: 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign. Letter from George W. Beale (son of General R. L. T. Beale)', dated 'July 13th, 1863', 'Four Miles Northwest of Williamsport, MD.', salutation 'Dearest Mother', signed 'G. W. Beale', footer '(Source: Southern Historical Society Papers, Vol. 11, p.320-327)'. The host is the hobbyist 'Gettysburg Discussion Group'. The /research/SHSP/ directory index lists 34 transcription files including shbeale.html. https:// on this host fails with CRYPT_E_REVOKED (revoked certificate), so only the http URL works. SCAN CHECK (independent of the first pass): archive.org item southernhistoric0011sout (full djvu text fetched, 1.7 MB). Its title page reads 'JANUARY TO DECEMBER, 1883' with the Kraus 1977 imprint, and its IA 'date' field says 1876 (series start, not the imprint). The contents line reads 'Gettysburg Campaign - A Soldier's Letter, by George W. Beale . 320'. The letter runs from the heading 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign. Letter from George W. Beale (son of General R. L. T. Beale)' on p. 320 to 'G. W. Beale.' on p. 327. IA page_numbers.json puts printed p. 320 at leaf 330 and p. 327 at leaf 337. A second, separate scan, sim_southern-historical-society-papers_1883-07_11_7 (the original July 1883 issue from microfilm), contains the same letter on pp. 320-327 (leaves 31-38). THREE-WAY WORD DIFF (gdg.org vs both scans, normalised): about 3,405 words on gdg vs 3,434 and 3,431 in the scans. Where both scans agree and gdg differs there are about 20 differences: gdg omits 'through', 'to', 'had' (twice), 'though', 'and', 'a' and a 'that'; reads 'withing' for 'within', 'until' for 'till', 'up' for 'us' ('found up upon the mountain'), 'be' for 'he', 'in' for 'at' ('fight in Hagerstown'), 'effected' for 'effects', 'Devine' for 'Divine', 'endeavored' for 'endeavoured', 'Your son' for print 'You son'; and doubles 'many of the'. It also silently drops the print's quotation marks around 'lady's man'. So it is a clean-ish transcription but not verbatim. DESCRIPTION CHECK (two concrete claims). (1) 'Confederate cavalryman's account of Stuart's movements': the letter says 'our brigade, with General F. Lee's and Hampton's, started from Lovdon' and 'General Stuart headed the expedition', then walks Salem (Thursday, June [25]), Thoroughfare Gap, Fairfax C.H., the Potomac ford, Rockville, Westminster, Hanover, Carlisle ('General Stuart sent an order for its surrender, which was refused'), the Gettysburg arrival and East Cavalry Field, and Hagerstown. (2) 'Transcribed from SHSP': confirmed by the scan text above, with the deviations listed. INDEPENDENT FACT CROSS-CHECKS. (a) OR vol. 27 pt. 2, Stuart's report (corpus id or27-2:0565, read-only cache historian-src/raw/or27/passages.jsonl) says at Rockville 'More than one hundred and twenty-five best United States model wagons' were taken, with about 400 prisoners. Beale writes 'nearly two hundred wagons' and 'about 12,000 ... mules', so he exaggerates. The surrender demand at Carlisle, refused and then shelling, matches. Stuart names 'Lieut. Col. W. H. Payne, Fourth Virginia Cavalry' captured at Hanover, which matches Beale's 'Colonel Payne'. Stuart says the column moved out 'At 1 o'clock at night' against Beale's '3 o'clock A. M.'. Stuart's 'My advance reached Gettysburg July 2' is consistent with the letter. (b) R. L. T. Beale, History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry (1899, archive.org historyofninthvi00beal): the roster lists 'Beale, George W ... First Lieutenant. Twice wounded', and the narrative says 'G. W. Beale was elected lieutenant in Company C'. The same book narrates 'Lieutenant Beale and Sergeant Richard Washington were leading' the charge on the guns near Hagerstown, with Washington found dead, and 'Lieutenant Beale was ordered to see that the remains ... were safely conveyed across the Potomac', matching the letter's Washington passage. (c) SHSP vol. 11 itself says R. L. T. Beale 'carried into the Ninth Virginia Cavalry his four sons'. This confirms the entry's '9th Virginia Cavalry' label, which the letter never states outright; the letter says 'the Thirteenth and Ninth Virginia ... were ordered to charge' at Hanover and 'This regiment and the Thirteenth' on 3 July. No other entry in entries.json shares this URL key. Entry 596 is the father's 1899 regimental history, a different work.

rationale.evidence: Fetched http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/sites/blogdivided/files/2018/06/Anna-Fosdick-recollection.pdf (301 to https; HTTP 200; application/pdf; full file 1,080,976 bytes, re-fetched because the earlier probe was truncated). It has 3 pages that are images only, so I rendered and read them. Page 1: a foreword, 'The incidents related in this article, THE ARGESHEIMER FAMILY, are given from my own knowledge', signed Mrs. Anna M. M. Fosdick, 14 June 1937. Page 2: 'The Argesheimer Family by Mrs. Anna (Argesheimer) Fosdick' covering her father John Henry Argesheimer, a German-born army bandmaster, and her mother Harriet Lavenia Wallace (born 1837 at Gettysburg); the only Carlisle shelling content is a short passage in which she says she remembers hearing her mother describe wounded exchanged Union prisoners being fed in the Carlisle market when Rebel shells began bursting over it. Page 3: the children listed with 'Anna Mary Magdalene (Mrs. C. H. Fosdick, Carey Block, Cheyenne), born at Carlisle, Pennsylvania, January 6, 1864', that is six months after the shelling of 1 July 1863, then the family's move to Fort D. A. Russell, Wyoming in 1875. So the author was not an eyewitness: the description 'Carlisle woman's recollection of the shelling' is false; this is secondhand family tradition from her mother, recorded in 1937 in a family history, in a few sentences. I did not identify the Dickinson blog post that hosts the PDF.

Russell, Wyoming, and Cheyenne, with no more on 1863. So Anna was born six months after the event and is repeating her mother's story: second-hand, not 'a Carlisle woman's recollection of the shelling'. Appleton, 1893, 439 pages', full view. Read the Internet Archive Cornell scan cu31924022024081 (item page HTTP 200; metadata; djvu.txt 942,091 bytes). Chapter V, 'Life during the Civil War and its sequence, 1862-1866' (opens p. 245), has a summary that reads, in part, 'The Emergency - I enter an artillery company ... I see rebel scouts near Harrisburg - The shelling of Carlisle ... Stewart Patterson ... The battle of Gettysburg - The retreat of Lee'. Running head '254 MEMOIRS.' marks the page: it is mid-account of the Carlisle shelling of 1 July 1863, with his captain Landis saying shells would not hurt 'till they hit you' and a shell-burst by a lamp-post, and p. 255 continues the anecdote about Theodore Fassitt's horse. So the PA254 anchor lands on a real Carlisle passage. Claim 1: militia volunteer in the emergency campaign (artillery company under Gen. W. F. Smith, Landis' battery). Claim 2: Gettysburg relevance is campaign only: Leland writes that, as raw recruits, they were 'not put under fire at Gettysburg, but kept in Smith's reserve' (p. 262), and he describes campfires seen the night before the battle. His account of Carlisle is a union-side counterpart to entries 598 and 604; Patterson, named in his chapter summary, served in the same battery.

rationale.evidence: The listed URL (dq=, pg=PA254) was not fetched (robots). The bare page https://books.google.com/books?id=O7Ud9eFYGWcC (HTTP 200, 67,529 bytes) shows 'Memoirs, Charles Godfrey Leland, D. Appleton, 1893, 439 pages', full view with PDF/EPUB download. I read two IA scans of the same Appleton edition: Cornell cu31924022024081 (474 images, OCR 942,091 bytes; ends at p. 439 with the Appleton advertisements) and the Library of Congress memoirs00lela (472 images, OCR 1,094,894 bytes; page map puts printed p. 254 at leaf 272). The chapter '1862-1866' has the running head 'Life during the Civil War'. On p. 251-252 Leland says he went as a 'full private' in an artillery company whose captain was 'a dealer in cutlery named Landis'; the Carlisle shelling starts at the foot of p. 253 ('Hearing that the rebels were threatening Carlisle, we were sent thither on a forced march of sixteen miles') and p. 254 holds the lamp-post and grape-shot passage and Landis's remark about shells, so PA254 lands in the middle of the account. On p. 262 he says 'we were not put under fire at Gettysburg, but kept in Smith's reserve'. Independent cross-check: Wingate's history (pp. 229-231, Cornell scan) quotes Leland's Memoirs with page cites 'p. 254', 'p. 256' (Stuart Patterson's right-hand fingers cut away by a shell) and 'p. 257' (his brother's wound), all of which match the passages in the Appleton scans, confirming that pagination. Accuracy of the entry's wording ('Writer and militia volunteer's account of the emergency campaign'): yes. Caution: Leland's chronology is loose (he says the rebels 'had been before us, and partially burned the barracks' whereas Garnett and Stuart place the barracks fire during the July 1 bombardment) and he writes 'about ten thousand rebel regulars' where Garnett says about 1,500. Provenance: House Divided's post lists 'Charles Godfrey Leland memoir (Union)' with this exact URL.

W. F. Smith's report as quoted by Wingate on p. 225 (Landis' battery replied with three); and 'Hans Breitman (Charles S. Leland)' rode astride a gun on the way. rationale.evidence: Fetched http://openn.library.upenn.edu/Data/0010/html/00_J91_42_P4529j.html (301/308 to https, HTTP 200, 190,738 B) and the TEI XML (73,263 B). Page title 'Journal of Charles Ashmead Schaeffer', call no. *00 J91.42 P4529j, 'Krauth Memorial Library Archives' (Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia, hosted by Penn's OPenn), date 'From 1862 to 1863'; summary says 'military combat in Carlisle, Pennsylvania'. The listed fragment #a60r exists (anchor in the HTML, table of contents 'fol. 60r - July 1, 1863'). Downloaded and read the web JPGs for fols. 59v, 60r, 60v, 61v, 62r (1028_0119, 0120, 0121, 0123, 0124). Fol. 59v: after joining Capt. Landis' artillery company he mustered, reached Harrisburg, was at Fort Washington until 1 July. Fol. 60r (dated July 1): marched toward Carlisle, reached it about 6 P.M., fed at the market house, about 7 P.M. heard the cry that the rebels were coming. Fol. 60v: shells fell in the square, his gun fired, Cpl. Patterson's fingers were struck. Fol. 61v-62r: firing ended about 11:30 P.M.; a man named Colladay died after amputation; at 3 A.M. three more shells; rebels reported gone; a hindsight sentence says they numbered 6,000-7,000 against 2,100. Two concrete description claims checked: (a) digitized manuscript diary: yes (185 image files, no text); (b) Union volunteer during the emergency: yes, Landis' battery (= entries 595/599). Independent corroboration of identity: Wikipedia via search result says Schaeffer served in the 'First Pennsylvania Battery' and was University of Iowa president 1887-98 (secondary, not fetched by me).

rationale.evidence: Fetched the PDF at the listed URL (301 to https, HTTP 200, cached 49,732 B, 2 pages, sha256 bd2c3776...) and extracted the text layer. Caption: 'Hanna Culver from Carlisle to her brother Joseph F. Culver, Joseph Franklin Culver collection, Special Collection, University of Iowa library. Her brother was serving with the 129th Illinois Infantry in Tennessee.' Letter: 'East Villa July 9th /63 Dear Brother'. Claims checked: (a) occupation: Jenkins entered about eleven on Saturday (27 June), Ewell's main body arrived at three, Ewell's corps left on Tuesday morning along the Baltimore pike, citizens' stores sacked; (b) shelling: Smith's brigade arrived about seven on Wednesday evening, 'Stuarts gorillas under command of Fitzhugh Lee' threw shells, a flag of truce was refused, a general cannonade lasted about four hours, gasworks and garrison burned, 'Seventeen of our Soldiers were wounded two of whom had a limb amputated'. It also reports 'Gen. Lee has been so badly beaten at Gettiesburg', and that relatives had gone to see the battleground. Family context cross-checked on the University of Iowa blog for entry 618: the father Joseph Culver (72) lived in Carlisle's East Ward. The Blog Divided category page (fetched) lists this PDF as 'Culver Family Correspondence - Hanna Culver's July 9, 1863 letter detailing the occupation and shelling'.

Dateline 'Lewistown, Pa / July 15th, 1863', salutation 'Prof. Marshal', signed 'G. D. Chenoweth'. (4) Description check, claim 1 ('account of the Confederate occupation'): the letter says the rebels entered Carlisle in strong force, 'twelve thousand', on Saturday evening, pitched tents by Dr. Johnson's door and on the campus, and plundered flour, groceries, dry goods and shoes. Claim 2 (the invasion): the rebels left on news of an attack 'near Gettysburg'; militia from Harrisburg came in; the rebel cavalry then shelled the town until three in the morning after a flag of truce to General Smith was refused. The description is accurate as far as it goes. (5) Scan vs transcript: I compared the closing paragraph on scan p.3 (faint at 110 dpi) and the first lines on p.2. The hand clearly reads 'Our Army gained a complete victory over Lee at Gettysburg', 'News has just arrived that the rebel Army have escaped across the Potomac' and 'Our prospects were never so bright'; less clearly 'college will open as usual in Sept.' and 'dispensing with a part of the exercises'. The host transcript prints 'And Army', 'now has just announced', 'Our force feels we're never so bright', 'in July' and 'a form of the exams'. On p.2 the hotel name looks like 'Pleas't hotel' where the transcript has 'Pealy Hotel' (less certain). (6) Provenance of the entry: the one-line description is the caption in Cooper Wingert's House Divided blog post of 11 June 2018 (entry 639): 'George Chenoweth Letter - Carlisle civilian's account'. The part header's 'compiled by Dickinson College House Divided Project' is loose: the item is hosted by Dickinson Archives & Special Collections.
rationale.rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 manuscript letter by an adult with four children, so the author was born well before 1850 and died more than 70 years ago whatever his exact dates (his death date was not looked up). The text is public domain by date. Host: the item page footer reads 'Copyright (c) 2020 Archives & Special Collections at Dickinson College. All rights reserved.' (live page: 2025); the PDF cover sheet carries contact details only, no reuse terms; the typed transcript is the Archives' own work. Tier A2 because the host's notice and transcription rights are unresolved, not because the text is in doubt. Quote from the manuscript scan, not from the host's transcript.
rationale.extraction_notes: Text source: scan pp.2-3 of the PDF (about 750 words of 1863 prose; roughly 600 words concern the occupation and shelling, the rest family news and war news). The PDF text layer on pp.4-5 is the Archives' typed transcript and has misreads, so use it to locate passages only and transcribe quotes by hand from the scan (adapter: manual-transcription; pdf-text read but not trusted). The scan is clear enough to read at 110 dpi. Cite the live page, not the dead URL. The writer's weekdays are unreliable (see issues); do not derive dates from them.
issues: Second-hand: he says he left Carlisle on the last train 'Thursday night' before the rebels entered and returned afterwards; the occupation and shelling are reported from others. Attribute accordingly; the entry's 'Carlisle civilian's account of the Confederate occupation' is true of the town, not of what he saw.

Dickinson's typed transcript misreads the manuscript in the closing paragraph (checked against the scan): 'And Army' for 'Our Army', 'now has just announced' for 'News has just arrived', 'Our force feels we're never so bright' for 'Our prospects were never so bright' (these three clear); probably also 'in July' for 'in Sept.' and 'a form of the exams' for 'a part of the exercises' (less clear at the resolution I used). Quote from the scan.

Weekday slip: he puts both the militia's arrival and the shelling on 'Tuesday evening'; entry 624 and the Dickinson catalogue place the shelling on the evening of 1 July 1863 (a Wednesday). Do not treat his weekdays as dates.

Writer identity: the live catalogue tags 'Chenoweth, George Durbin' (Dickinson class of 1868, per the live person page), but the letter names 'Durbin & Alexander' in the third person as freshmen and speaks of four children, a wife and boarding in Lewistown, so the writer is an older man, probably the father. I could not verify the father's full name or office; do not attribute the letter to the son.
The twelve-thousand figure is hearsay; do not use it as a strength figure.
Listed URL is dead since the Dickinson Archives site migration; the title's '(civilian)' is the list's own gloss, not part of the title.
The footer notice 'All rights reserved' is site-wide boilerplate and no per-item licence was found, so a human rights decision precedes any quoting.

description_issues: Retrospective (67 years) and largely second-hand: Hillman says he and his mother left Carlisle in early June and were in New York when the shelling happened; most of the account is his father's stories and hearsay (a telegram from Gov. Wayback: I fetched web.archive.org/web/20231207200308/https://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war-resources/carlisle-sentinel-%E2%80%9Ctheodore-m-johnson-tells-civil-war-days-carlisle%E2%80%9D (HTTP 200, title 'Carlisle Sentinel, "Theodore M. Johnson Tells of Civil War Days in Carlisle"', 2 pages, date June 1924, location I-Original-1924-2) and the PDF capture web.archive.org/web/20240616012421id_/https://archives.dickinson.edu/sites/all/files/files_war/I-Original-1924-2.pdf (725,723 bytes, sha256 22c26181c788..., 2 pages). (2) PDF: p.1 cover sheet; p.2 one JPEG (781 x 4316 px) of a newspaper clipping, no text layer. I extracted the image and read the whole clipping. Headline: 'Member of Class of '73 Here on a Visit' over 'Theodore M. Johnson Tells of Civil War Days in Carlisle'. Body: 'Speaking to a Sentinel reporter, Mr. Johnson told of some of his recollections of Civil War days'; he was 'a boy of about nine years' when the Confederates 'visited Carlisle and shelled the town'. Pencil note at the foot: 'From Sentinel, June 1924'. (3) Description check ('Recollection by the son of the Dickinson College president'): the article says he is the son of Dr. Herman M. Johnson, president of the college 1860 to 1868, and lived in the fourth section of East College. Two concrete claims verified: a shell struck the second-floor casement, 'the sixth from the East side', of East College, and another split a cherry tree in the back garden without exploding. Accurate. (4) Title/authorship: the list's 'Theodore M. Johnson, "Tells of Civil War Days in Carlisle," Carlisle Sentinel' turns the headline into an author and a title; the text is a reporter's piece quoting Johnson. Provenance: the description is the caption in Wingert's blog post (entry 639): 'Theodore M. Johnson account - (son of Dickinson College President Herman Johnson)'.
rationale.rights_basis: A US newspaper article published in June 1924 (archive metadata 'June 1924' plus the pencil note): a pre-1931 imprint, so public domain. Tier A2 rather than A1 because the only copy is Dickinson's scan of an undated, unpaged clipping with no masthead, the issue date was not confirmed from the Sentinel itself, and the page footer carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 Archives & Special Collections at Dickinson College. All rights reserved.'. The scan adds nothing copyrightable; a human clears the host notice.
rationale.extraction_notes: Image-only: no usable text layer. Transcribe the clipping by hand (roughly 900 words, part of it about the 1863 events and part about the president's term and Johnson's visit; adapter: manual-transcription) and have a second person check it. Cite as Carlisle Sentinel, June 1924 (undated clipping), interview with Theodore M. Johnson. The 1863 passages: the first shell passing over, the shell striking East College, the dud in the garden, the Confederate cavalry colonel posting a guard and taking meals with the Johnsons after the president gave the Masonic sign, and the Southern troops who had been students.
issues: Authorship: an unsigned Sentinel reporter's article quoting Johnson, not an article by Johnson; cite accordingly.
Date and page unconfirmed: the clipping has no masthead, date line or page; 'June 1924' is the archive's metadata and a pencil note. Find the issue before citing a day.
Retrospective: Johnson says he was about nine in 1863 and speaks 61 years later.

The Dickinson catalogue blurb says Johnson saw Rodes's division of Ewell's corps and Stuart's cavalry corps; the article names no unit or general (only 'the Confederate cavalry' and 'the colonel'). Do not import the blurb's identifications.
Conflicts with entry 621: Johnson puts Conway Wing Hillman beside him at the first shell; Hillman's 1930 letter (born 1856, by his own account in New York in June 1863) says he was away.
Listed link is dead; no live replacement found, only the Wayback capture.

Found the same Library of Congress scan on the Internet Archive: item oldmercersburg00woma, metadata fetched (identifier-ark ark:/13960/t6k07cb88, identical to the HathiTrust id loc.ark:/13960/t6k07cb88 in the entry; imagecount 350; title 'Old Mercersburg'; creator Woman's Club of Mercersburg; publisher Frank Allaben Genealogical Co.; date 1912). Downloaded the OCR text (oldmercersburg00woma_djvu.txt, 908,442 bytes, sha256 837ff9cd8c634d34...) and read the diary: the section is headed as Dr. Philip Schaff's reminiscences, taken from a special journal and edited by D. S. S. (his son), starts at printed p. 162 with an entry dated 'Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, June 26, 1863', then dated entries from June 14 through July 21 (printed pp. 162 to about 171; last page header found by OCR is 170). The slave-hunt is in the entry for Friday (June 26), printed p. 165 ('on a regular slave-hunt'), and the June 27 entry (pp. 165-166) describes the guerilla band driving off about five hundred sheep and twenty-one negroes, naming Sam Brooks. Claim checks: (1) 'Mercersburg diary describing a slave-hunt through the town' is true and sharp; (2) the date range 'June 16-27' is too narrow (the printed diary covers June 14 to July 21 and includes July 5-9 Confederate wounded from Gettysburg arriving at the Seminary and prisoners' remarks about the battle); (3) 'McNeill's Rangers' is NOT in Schaff's text: he writes of an independent guerilla band of fifty to eighty cavalry, mostly Marylanders and Virginians; the book names Captain McNeill only in a different passage (printed p. 157, July 1 raid, someone else's account). The identification of the band as McNeill's Rangers is a later historian's inference that I did not verify. HathiTrust seq=277 could not be checked; the Archive page_numbers.json maps printed p. 123 to leaf 221 and p. 191 to leaf 311, so p. 165 falls between leaf 263 and 285 depending on plates, which makes seq 277 plausible but unconfirmed.

rationale.evidence: Listed HathiTrust babel link NOT fetched (registry policy: bot-blocked, robots Disallow /cgi/). Same scan on the Internet Archive: item oldmercersburg00woma (title 'Old Mercersburg', creator Woman's Club of Mercersburg, publisher Frank Allaben Genealogical Co., New York, date 1912, 350 images, contributor Library of Congress, lccn 12017565, oclc 2652575). Its identifier-ark ark:/13960/t6k07cb88 equals the HathiTrust id in the entry (loc.ark:/13960/t6k07cb88). The HathiTrust catalog API (record 009569191) gives title Old Mercersburg, 1912, same lccn and oclc. I fetched the Archive OCR (908,442 bytes, sha256 837ff9cd8c634d34...) and the hOCR, and viewed the page image of leaf n276 (1-based leaf 277). It is printed p. 163, headed 'The Gettysburg Week / By Philip Schaff, D.D. / By Permission of David Schley Schaff, D.D.' The editor's note, signed D. S. S., says the reminiscences 'are taken from a special journal kept by Dr. Schaff during several weeks in July, 1863, and are given in the exact form in which he wrote them'. The first dated line is 'Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, June 26, 1863', and the entries start 'Sunday, June 14th'. The last entry is 'Tuesday, July 21st' (p. 170), so the entry's 'June 16-27' is a fragment. Concrete claim 1 (verified): the text says 'On Friday this guerilla band came to town on a regular slave-hunt, which presented the worst spectacle I ever saw in this war' (printed p. 165). The 27th is described as 'a sight as sad and mournful as the slave-hunt of yesterday', with twenty-one negroes driven through town. Claim 2 (verified): there is also a captured woman with two little children, and the named captive Sam Brooks, who 'split many a cord of wood for me'. Claim 3 (NOT in the text): 'McNeill's Rangers' is never named in the diary. Schaff writes 'an independent guerilla band of cavalry ... mostly Marylanders and Virginians', fifty to eighty men. In the same book the only McNeill passage is a different narrator's account of July 1 on p. 157, 'the celebrated Captain McNeill'. A separate chapter of the book, 'Mercersburg in War Times', corroborates a June 26 seizure of Black residents (names John Filkill, Findlay Cuff, Samuel Brooks) without naming the unit. So the unit identification is the list's inference, not Schaff's text. HathiTrust seq=277 is consistent with the diary's first page only if HathiTrust numbers the same LC images 1-based like the Archive (1-based leaf 277 = p. 163); not checkable.

Description check 1: in the chapter on Jenkins's occupation (mid-June 1863) Hoke writes that soldiers hunted Black residents, free and enslaved, and sent some south under guard; a well-known Black resident, Esquire Hall, was carried off behind a rebel horseman, Hoke fetched the Rev. Dr. B. S. Schneck, who went to Jenkins's headquarters and vouched that Hall was a long-time resident and not a fugitive, and Hall was released; Schneck said a Jenkins staff officer who had once heard him preach in Virginia helped. That is a captured Black resident freed through a Confederate connection, as the entry says. Check 2: the same passage has Jenkins telling Schneck he would not burn a hay stack because Lee's whole army was coming. Page check: counting lines between the OCR page numbers and the hOCR page index both put the Hall passage on leaf 44, which page_numbers.json labels printed page 38, matching the Google Books anchor PA38.

rationale.evidence: Fetched the entry URL over http (HTTP 200, 200 KB, last-modified 2010-09-04; robots.txt 404 so no restrictions): title and author match (Peter C. Vermilyea, 'The Effect of the Confederate Invasion of Pennsylvania on Gettysburg's African American Community'); about 89 footnotes; it opens with Elizabeth ('Old Liz') Butler. Fetched http://www.gdg.org/Gettysburg%20Magazine/gcontents.html: it lists this article last under 'Issue Number 24' of Gettysburg Magazine, before 'Issue Number 25'. Checked two concrete claims in the text: (a) flight: a section on the exodus of Gettysburg's Black residents northward as Lee's army approached, with named examples (Biggs left on July 1); (b) capture: Confederate seizure of Black residents (e.g. the June 16 capture of 30-40 women and children at Chambersburg freed at Greencastle), and Butler bound and gagged, then escaping. Also reports the 1860 and 1870 census change (186 Black residents in 1860, no more than 74 still there in 1870) and the burial work done by Basil Biggs after the battle. The entry's note that the magazine is edited but not formally peer-reviewed is consistent with the venue (not independently verified).

rationale.evidence: Fetched the entry URL over http (HTTP 200, 200,687 bytes, content-type text/html, Last-Modified Sat 04 Sep 2010, Server Apache; robots.txt is 404 so no restriction; no redirect to https). Title as the entry: 'The Effect of the Confederate Invasion of Pennsylvania on Gettysburg's African American Community', by Peter C. Vermilyea (an author box says he teaches history in Connecticut and is scholarship director at Gettysburg College's Civil War Institute). Description claim 1, 'flight': the text says Black residents of Gettysburg and south central Pennsylvania were fleeing north out of fear of capture, and later sections cover refuge in Harrisburg, Philadelphia and the Yellow Hill area. Description claim 2, 'capture': it describes mounted Confederates searching fields and houses for Black residents; the Greencastle incident of 16 June, in which 30 to 40 captured women and children were freed by townspeople; Longstreet's 1 July note to Pickett about bringing the captured 'contraband' along; and the author's estimate that at least fifty Adams County Black residents were sold in southern slave markets. The page ends with 89 numbered footnotes. Its first section follows Elizabeth ('Old Liz') Butler, aged about 53 in 1863. Venue check: the contents page lists this article under 'Issue Number 24', with Calliha, Jorgensen, Dougherty, O'Brien, Lade and Mahon articles. An independent web page (studycivilwar.wordpress.com, fetched) cites a passage found on this page as 'Gettysburg Magazine, Issue 24, p. 116'. rationale.evidence: Page HTTP 200 (280 KB, server-rendered) and TEI FD1006.xml (54 KB) fetched. Rachel Cormany lived in Chambersburg while her husband Samuel served in the 16th Pennsylvania Cavalry. There are 23 dated entries, 14 June to 6 July 1863. Check 1 (Jenkins's cavalry arriving): the 15 and 16 June entries describe the panic at Milroy's wagon train and then Confederate riders passing her window in the night; on 17 June she records seeing Gen. Jenkins, and an editor's footnote says his cavalry led the advance. Check 2 (capture of Black residents): on 16 June she writes that the Confederates hunted up the contrabands and drove them off in droves, women and children, including some colored people raised in town, and on 17 June that they were still carrying off 'darkeys' and some rode out with them behind the saddle. Check 3 (retreat from Gettysburg): the 5 July entry reports citizens capturing wagons of wounded and the rumour that the rebel army was retreating, and 6 July records Samuel's arrival. All of it is hearsay from Chambersburg, not an eyewitness account of the battle. Editors' footnotes (26) are interleaved on the page.

rationale.evidence: GET of the entry URL gave HTTP 200, 157,089 bytes, text/html, no redirect; robots.txt HTTP 404. The browser title is Letters of the Cormany Family, The War Years, The Valley of the Shadow; the page heading is Samuel and Rachel Cormany (1863) in the Franklin County diaries section. Content: a biography (Rachel born Bowman in Canada in 1836, Samuel born 1838 and raised in Chambersburg, married November 1860 after meeting at Otterbein, returned to Chambersburg August 1862, Samuel enlisted as second lieutenant in the 16th Pennsylvania Cavalry in September 1862) and two excerpt blurbs: Samuel's diary of service in the 16th Pennsylvania Cavalry in the Gettysburg Campaign, late June to early July 1863 (rumors of battle, then the battle, then pursuit and a chance to see his wife), and Rachel's diary of panic and occupation in Chambersburg. The cards that open the diaries are rendered by the page's JavaScript (component ids FD1007 and FD1006), so the static HTML has no anchors to them; I did not render the page. I fetched the Samuel diary page https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/diaries/FD1007 (HTTP 200): title Franklin County, Diary of Samuel Cormany (1863); daily entries June 30 to July 6 with seven footnotes. Two concrete checks of the description: the July 1 entry has him at Hanover hearing cannonading and then musketry toward Gettysburg and a rumor of battle; the July 3 entry reports the heaviest cannonading he had ever heard, about 1:30 to 4 pm, with his squadron on the right of the line; footnote 7 confirms the 16th Pennsylvania pursued the retreating Confederates toward Chambersburg and the July 6 entry has him leaving the column to reach his wife and child. Cross-check against the OR order of battle (read in the Archive OCR, p. 167): the 16th Pennsylvania Cavalry (Lt. Col. John K. Robison) is listed in the Third Brigade (Col. J. Irvin Gregg), Second Division, Cavalry Corps, whereas the July 2 entry names the 2nd Brigade, 2nd Division; the diary's and the OR's brigade number disagree (cause not determined). The first pass said the Stuart explanation sits on the July 2 entry; in fact footnote 4 (Stuart's ride) is attached to the July 1 entry.

Check 1 (horse seizures): 17 June says the Rebels are scouring the country for horses; 19 June says they are scouring Waynesboro, Greencastle, Mercersburg and Finkstown for horses, cattle and Negroes; 25 June reports them scouring Franklin, Cumberland, York and Adams counties. Check 2 (the army's passage): 24 June reports Lee's army at Shippensburg, 27 June about 20,000 marching past towards Baltimore, 28 June Ewell's and Longstreet's men going down the pike to Carlisle, 30 June immense baggage trains with 42 guns; on 2 July about 1,000 cavalry camp on the family's fields and take chickens, bees and 150 bushels of corn paid in Confederate scrip. Check 3 (rumours of the battle): 3 July he has heard rumours of a great battle about Gettysburg, 4 July 'still fighting over the mountain', 5 July captured wagons of wounded. On 7 and 8 July he visits the battlefield (unburied dead, unexploded shells, trodden fields). He is plainly a farmer (plowing corn, planting tobacco, horses sent to the mountains), though no text states it.

rationale.evidence: Listed URL https://valley.newamericanhistory.org/war/letters-and-diaries/franklin/stouffer returns 200 (155,024 bytes), title 'Letters of the Stouffer Family - The War Years - The Valley of the Shadow'; heading 'Stouffer Family (1861-1865)'. The page's tab counts read War 12, Aftermath 1, and its embedded data lists letters F6500 to F6509 (ten) and diaries FD7001 (Eliza R. Stouffer, 1863) and FD5500 (Amos Stouffer, 1863); the Franklin index (entry 651) says 'ten wartime letters (1861-1865)' plus the two 1863 diaries, which is the entry's wording. I fetched all ten letter pages (200): dated 20 Dec 1861 to 17 Aug 1864; F6506 is Jacob Stouffer to his daughter Mary, 5 July 1863, describing the rebel army camping around his farm, Lee's headquarters in Shetter's woods and the wagon trains and artillery marching toward Gettysburg on 30 June. The Aftermath tab adds an eleventh letter, F6510 (Benjamin Stouffer to Emma, 16 April 1865). Diaries read: FD5500 has daily entries for 1863 including the rebels in Franklin County from 15 June, hearsay of the Gettysburg battle on 3-5 July, and a trip to the cemetery dedication on 18-20 November; FD7001 is Eliza's trip diary of 12 June to 10 July 1863 in Lancaster County with rumours of the invasion and no battle text. The entry's description (ten family letters plus the 1863 diaries of Amos and Eliza) therefore matches the host's own count; the collection holds eleven letters if the Aftermath item is counted. Re-verified in a second run on 2026-10-04 with fresh fetches into a new cache (tmp/sources-v2/r3b-recheck/): the page is still 200 with the same ten letter ids F6500 to F6509 and diary ids FD5500 and FD7001, tab counts War 12 and Aftermath 1 (page weight differs between fetches, 155,024 bytes on 2026-10-01 against 44,440 on 2026-10-04, with the same ids and text); F6500 is Eliza R. Stouffer to Anna Hoover, December 20, 1861, F6509 is Eliza R. Stouffer to her 'Sister in Faith,' August 17, 1864, and the Aftermath page lists F6510 (Benjamin Stouffer to Emma V. Stouffer, April 16, [1865]); F6506 (Jacob Stouffer to Mary R. Stouffer, July 5, 1863) was re-read and does say the rebels entered Chambersburg on 15 June, Lee had his headquarters in A. Shetter's woods and about 700 army wagons passed toward Gettysburg on Tuesday 30 June. CORRECTION to the first run: the diary of Amos Stouffer (FD5500, re-read this run) is not only hearsay: after rumours of the battle on 3 to 5 July it records on Tuesday 7 July 1863 that he went to the battlefield (he got there about 11 o'clock and saw a great many unburied rebels and some Union soldiers), on 8 July that he went all over the battle field, and on 18 to 20 November the trip to the cemetery dedication. So the collection reaches the battle only through hearsay and a post-battle visit; there is still no eyewitness account of the fighting. The relevance field is therefore raised from campaign-only to campaign-and-battle.

Page 5 shows 'Vicksburg Taken!' in column 1 and the Ewell and 'Rebels Jubilant' columns beside it, matching the transcript, and the creases the transcriber notes. Check 1 (headline): the page 5 article is headed 'The Invasion! The Whole Rebel Army in Franklin County!' (subheads include 47,000 Pass Through Chambersburg and Lee's Headquarters at Shetter's Woods). Check 2 (Ewell's requisition): under 'Ewell Supplies' it prints Ewell's requisitions dated June 24, 1863 (5,000 suits of clothing, 100 saddles, 100 bridles, 5,000 bushels of grain, leather, horseshoes, lead, 50,000 lbs of bread and more), says the citizens resolved not to comply, and that the Rebels then helped themselves. The article also covers Jenkins's return on 22 June, Lee at Shetter's grove, the Rebel march on Harrisburg, and Lee's retreat across South Mountain after Gettysburg. Page 1 has the account of Jenkins's first occupation (from 17 June) with a $300,000 loss estimate; page 4 has editors' and battle material (a short Gettysburg account praising Meade, and dispatches). 177 '[illegible]' markers appear across the transcript (31 inside the main article), from the page crease.

rationale.evidence: The Perseus link was not fetched because www.perseus.tufts.edu/robots.txt disallows all paths (earlier probe). Its table of contents lists 'XVII. The Correspondence of General R. E. Lee. Chancellorsville to Gettysburg - March to August, 1863. A pathetic array of evidence from the War Records, by Colonel Wm. H. Palmer 148'; the heading in the volume reads 'THE CORRESPONDENCE OF GEN. ROBT. E. LEE. Chancellorsville to Gettysburg - March to August, 1863'. Per the Archive's page_numbers.json, p.148 is leaf 162, p.155 is leaf 169, p.156 (next article) is leaf 170. Content read: a table of abstracts with OR page references (Series I, Vol. XXV pt. II, then Vol. XXVII pt. III), each line 'sender, date, page, addressee' plus a gist: e.g. 'R. E. Lee, April 20 ... to Davis. Insufficiency of cavalry', 'General Lee to General J. E. B. Stuart, June 22, 1863, page 913', 'General Lee to Davis, June 23, page 923', 'General Lee, Williamsport, June 25, 1863, to Davis'. Addressees also include Seddon, Cooper, A. P. Hill, Stuart; there are also letters from Seddon, Davis, Cooper, Jenkins to others. At the end (p.155): 'Mr. Davis' Letter to General Lee, June 28, 1863 ... was entrusted to a courier, who was captured by Captain Dahlgren, of General Meade's staff', and 'General Lee first learned that his suggestions would not be entertained by reading Mr. President Davis' letter in the New York Herald and New York Tribune', then 'GENERAL LEE RESIGNED IN AUGUST.' The compiler is named in the editor's note as 'Colonel William H. Palmer, formerly Chief of Staff of General A. P. Hill'; the editor's framing says the correspondence shows the army 'debilitated from being insufficiently fed'.

reviews.written: 1863-06-12 (dispatches and orders dated Camp near Falmouth, Va.)
issues: Live eHistory link not verified (host not fetched); only a 2021 Wayback capture of the same URL matches the scan page.

reviews.evidence: IA pt. 3 OCR leaf 79 = printed p. 73 (n78), running head 'Chap. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC. UNION.' with page number 73. The page carries the tail of a Butterfield dispatch begun on p. 72 to the Commanding Officer First Corps (June 12, 1863: he is to assume command of the right wing and 'move with your corps up to the vicinity of Bealeton'), signed 'DAN L. BUTTERFIELD, Major-General, Chief of Staff'. Then two orders dated Camp near Falmouth, Va., June 12, 1863: S. Williams to the Commanding Officer Third Corps ('take possession of the fords assigned you to hold to-night') and Butterfield to the Commanding Officer Sixth Corps ('quietly withdraw your forces to the north bank of the Rappahannock'). A Wayback capture of the exact eHistory URL (web.archive.org/web/20210613033552) is titled 'War of the Rebellion: Serial 045 Page 0073 Chapter XXXIX. CORRESPONDENCE, ETC. - UNION' and carries the same text. eHistory itself was not requested.
reviews.extraction_notes: Pointer entry, no new text: the page is already in the IA OCR the historian ingests. Three documents on the page, the first beginning on p. 72. Split by the 'Headquarters ... Camp near Falmouth' datelines. For quoting use the IA scan, not eHistory. The eHistory capture is from 2021, so the live link is unconfirmed.

reviews.evidence: IA pt. 3 leaf 219 = printed p. 213 (n218). I viewed the page image. It carries the end of a letter from Brig. Gen. Rufus Ingalls, Chief Quartermaster, to Maj. Gen. D. Butterfield (dated Camp near Fairfax Court-House, June 19, 1863; the opening is on p. 212): 'I think it will be correct at the present time to place the number of wagons now with this army at about 4,000.' Then an '[Inclosure.] Recapitulation of the number of officers and enlisted men, cavalry and artillery horses, wagons, and means of transportation in the Army of the Potomac', by corps, with totals of 7,937 officers and 134,161 men, 4,302 army wagons (total row), and a second table of wagons per officers and men. The page has no dispatch beginning on it. A Wayback capture of the eHistory URL (20210625063308) is titled 'Serial 045 Page 0213 ... CORRESPONDENCE, ETC. - UNION' and carries the same letter tail and tables.
reviews.extraction_notes: The table OCR is one value per line (about 209 lines) and unusable; use the page image or eHistory's table, and do not parse the OCR. The OCR misreads a penciled note: it gives '8,750' where the page says 3,750 (75,000 men = 3,750 wagons). Letter opens on p. 212. For the Historian this page is a statistical return, useful only as a cross-reference for army transport.

reviews.evidence: p. 353: June 27 at the Potomac crossings: Butterfield to Capt. Turnbull, Edwards Ferry (1 p.m.), Benham to Williams (8.35 p.m.), Crawford to Williams (9.25 a.m.: 'My command is crossing'), and Butterfield to Hooker 3.30 p.m. relaying Stahel's question whether to send cavalry from Middletown 'toward Emmitsburg and Gett[ysburg]'. reviews.written: 1863-06-27 (four dispatches of that day at the Potomac crossings)

reviews.evidence: IA pt. 3 leaf 359 = printed p. 353 (n358), running head 'CORRESPONDENCE, ETC. UNION.' with page number 353. Four June 27, 1863 items at the Potomac crossings: Butterfield (Headquarters, Frederick, 1 p.m.) to Capt. Turnbull at Edwards Ferry asking whether the Sixth Corps has crossed and for Crawford's Pennsylvania Reserves; Benham (8.35 p.m.) to Williams reporting about two-thirds of the Sixth Corps across; Crawford (9.25 a.m.): 'My command is crossing'; and Butterfield to Hooker at Harper's Ferry (3.30 p.m.): 'General Stahel desires to know if he shall withdraw his cavalry from Middletown, to send toward Emmitsburg and Gettysburg. Two regiments already gone toward those points.' A Wayback capture of the eHistory URL (20210622150753) is titled 'Serial 045 Page 0353' and carries the same text.
reviews.extraction_notes: Four short, separate documents; split by the datelines. The printed order is 1 p.m., 8.35 p.m., 9.25 a.m., 3.30 p.m., not strictly chronological, so do not assume page order equals time order. Mentions Gettysburg once (Stahel's question). For quoting use the IA scan, not eHistory.

reviews.evidence: IA pt. 3 leaf 464 = printed p. 458 (n463), running head 'N. C., VA., W. VA., MD., PA., ETC. [Chap. XXXIX.', an even page, with the page number 458. The page opens with the end of a dispatch signed 'O. O. HOWARD, Major-General' ('Enemy reported to be advancing from York (Ewell's corps). The First and Eleventh Corps are engaged with Hill's forces. Have ordered General Sickles to push forward.'). Then 'Hdqrs. Army of the Potomac, July 1, 1863 - 12 m.' from Geo. G. Meade to General Couch, Harrisburg ('The enemy are advancing on Gettysburg - Hill, from Cashtown; Ewell, from Heidlersburg'). Then 'Circular. Headquarters Army of the Potomac, Taneytown, July 1, 1863' (fall back to Pipe Creek if attacked; Reynolds to withdraw from Gettysburg). A Wayback capture of the eHistory URL (20210617162555) is titled 'Serial 045 Page 0458 N. C., VA., W. VA., MD., PA., ETC. Chapter XXXIX.' and carries the same text.
reviews.extraction_notes: Page starts mid-dispatch (Howard's, begun on p. 457). Third item is the Taneytown (Pipe Creek) circular, which is the most quoted text here; check its pages against the scan. Quote from the IA scan, not eHistory.

reviews.evidence: p. 586: Listed note ('Includes Third Corps report from Mechanicstown, July 7') is correct: line 7 reads 'Headquarters Third Corps, Mechanicstown, July 7, 1863 - 6.20 p.m. ... General: I have the honor to state that this corps moved from its position at Gettysburg this morning at 3 o'[clock]', signed Birney, to Sedgwick. Also French to Williams (Frederick), two Howard wires (Middletown 6.20 p.m., 9 p.m.).
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 592 (page+6). Third Corps march-day report; useful for the retreat from the field. Note verified.

reviews.written: 1863-07-07 (all dispatches on the page are dated July 7, 1863; contemporaneous, printed 1889)
issues: Template description 'printed chronologically for June 3-August 3, 1863' is generic.
'Third Corps report' is really a dispatch to Sedgwick, not a formal report.
Historian corpus row p0586.4 has the wrong signer (Warren instead of Howard) and p0586.1 carries the OCR place 'Mechcmicstown'.
reviews.evidence: Archive scan, printed p.586 = leaf 592 (page_numbers.json); page image viewed: folio 586, running head 'N. C., VA., W. VA., MD., PA., ETC. [Chap. XXXIX.'. Claim 1 verified: 'Headquarters Third Corps, Mechanicstown, July 7, 1863 - 6.20 p. m.', Birney to Maj. Gen. Sedgwick: 'this corps moved from its position at Gettysburg this morning at 3 o'clock', reached St. Joseph's College at 10 a.m. Claim 2 (march away from Gettysburg) is the same text. Also on the page: close of a Warren dispatch begun on p.585, French to Williams (Frederick City, July 7), Howard to Meade (Middletown, 6.20 p.m.), and the start of an Eleventh Corps dispatch of 9 p.m. Union side is right: Part III Union section runs pp.3-857. Wayback capture 2021-06-20 of the listed eHistory URL is titled 'Serial 045 Page 0586 ... Chapter XXXIX.' and shows the same text.
reviews.extraction_notes: OCR is good but the page opens and closes mid-dispatch: Warren's closing lines belong to p.585, and the Eleventh Corps 9 p.m. dispatch is signed O. O. HOWARD at the top of p.587. OCR error 'Mechcmicstown' (printed 'Mechanicstown'). The historian row or27-3:p0586.4 gives signer G. K. WARREN for the 9 p.m. Eleventh Corps dispatch; the scan shows Howard signed it (Warren's signature on p.587 belongs to the next dispatch, 10.30 p.m. to Howard). Scan URL for humans: https://archive.org/details/warofrebellion273unit/page/n591/mode/1up (resolves to the item; the page view is driven by script).

reviews.evidence: p. 673: Page image fetched from the Archive (n678, leaf 679) and viewed: two pen sketches of Union lines (2d Corps Hays', 5th Corps Crawford and Griffin, 6th Corps Sedgwick, Ayres, 'Pike') under the running head 'CHAP. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-UNION. 673'; OCR text is 82 characters. The sketch illustrates a July 13 Third Corps letter on p. 672 ('The lines will then run thus').
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 679 (page+6). A plate: nothing to ingest as text; cite as a figure only.

reviews.written: No text on the page. The sketches illustrate Sykes's letter of 1863-07-13, 4 p.m. on p.672 (contemporaneous, printed 1889)
issues: Description wrongly says the page is a transcribed page of dispatches; it is two sketch diagrams.
The registry's structural check for this page used the historian's mis-paged rows; the true page of those dispatches is p.674.
The printed head on p.672 reads 'Third Corps' over Sykes's (Fifth Corps) signature; recorded as printed.
reviews.evidence: Printed p.673 = leaf 679. Page image viewed: head 'CHAP. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-UNION. 673', then two boxed pen sketches (top: lines labelled '2d Corps, Hays', '5th Corps, Crawford', 'Griffin', 'Barn', 'Pike'; bottom: '6th Corps, Sedgwick', 'Ayres' 2d Div., 5th Corps', Hays, Crawford, Griffin) and the signature mark '43 R R-VOL XXVII, PT III'; the Archive OCR for the leaf is 74 characters. The page before (p.672, image viewed) prints a letter headed 'Headquarters Third Corps, July 13, 1863-4 p.m.', signed GEO. SYKES to General Humphreys, with 'The lines will then run thus:*' and the footnote '*See sketch on opposite page.' The Wayback capture of the listed eHistory URL (2021-06-24) shows only the word 'MAP' and the signature mark, no dispatches. So the list's 'Transcribed page of Union dispatches, orders, telegrams and returns' is false for this page; the Union side comes from the running head.
reviews.extraction_notes: Nothing to extract; the page is image-only. Do not cite p.673 for any dispatch. The 5 dispatches the historian corpus lists under p.673 (or27-3:p0673.1-.5, leaf 679) are really on printed p.674 (leaf 680): that leaf's text holds Howard's 6.35 p.m. note, Wadsworth's report, and S. Williams's three July 13 notes. P.673 is a plate and p.674 has no row, so the registry structural check ('5 dispatches begin on this page') rests on mis-paged rows; the running head 'UNION' is the correct side evidence.

reviews.evidence: p. 773: July 27: Warren to Haupt, Warrenton, 9 p.m. (Rappahannock Station); two Army of the Potomac circulars (sick and wounded; resignations accepted only on a surgeon's certificate); Schenck to Halleck, 11.15 a.m. (New York 30-day militia expiring). Head 'CORRESPONDENCE, ETC. UNION.', folio 773.
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 779 (page+6). Two numbered circulars and two telegrams.

reviews.written: 1863-07-27 (all items dated July 27, 1863; contemporaneous, printed 1889)
issues: Template description only; the page is not about Gettysburg itself (late July, Rappahannock Station, militia garrisons).
reviews.evidence: Printed p.773 = leaf 779; image header viewed: 'Chap. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-UNION. 773'. Text (OCR, cross-read with the 2021-06-24 eHistory capture): Warren to General Haupt, Warrenton, July 27, 9 p.m., about taking the south bank at Rappahannock Station (pontoons ordered up by rail); two Army of the Potomac circulars of July 27 (sick and wounded to the rear under Surgeon Letterman; no resignations accepted except on surgeon's certificate); Schenck to Halleck, Baltimore, July 27, 11.15 a.m., New York thirty-days' militia expiring, asks for the Eighth New York Heavy Artillery. Union side confirmed. The list's generic 'dispatches, orders, telegrams' wording fits. Wayback capture titled 'Serial 045 Page 0773 Chapter XXXIX. CORRESPONDENCE. ETC. -UNION.'
reviews.extraction_notes: OCR defects to expect: 'hank' for 'bank', 'in £he estima-tion', stray quotation mark after 'An-derson,'. The eHistory transcription has 'chef engineer' for 'chief engineer', so it is not verbatim. The page is about the Army of the Potomac's post-campaign administration, not the battle.

reviews.evidence: p. 843: Page prints 'ADDENDA.' (line 7) after the end of Le Duc's letter, then Quartermaster-General Meigs to Capt. R. N. Scott, Washington, December 6, 1878 (copies of June 1863 correspondence with Ingalls) with an inclosure 'August 3, 1863 - Abstract of papers relating to horses lost or abandoned'. This is the start of the Union Addenda (pp. 843-857), not the chronological June 3-Aug. 3 series.
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 849 (page+6). Editorial Addenda, 1878 transmittal; public-domain government correspondence but outside the 1863 window.

reviews.written: Mixed: end of Le Duc's letter of 1863-08-18; Meigs to Capt. R. N. Scott 1878-12-06 (compiler's correspondence, retrospective); inclosure dated 1863-08-03 abstracting June-July 1863 letters
issues: Label 'Union / Confederate (section transition)' is false: Union only; the Confederate section starts at p.858.
Template date range June 3-August 3, 1863 is wrong for this page, which holds an August 18, 1863 letter and a December 6, 1878 letter.
Page is about horses lost in the June 1863 march from Falmouth, not the fighting at Gettysburg.
reviews.evidence: Printed p.843 = leaf 849; header viewed: 'Chap. XXXIX.] 843 CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-UNION.' Page content (OCR plus the footnote read in the image): the end of Lt. Col. W. G. Le Duc's letter (its heading on p.841 reads 'Camp near Germantown, Va., August 18, 1863', to Gen. M. C. Meigs, about Eleventh Corps horses lost on the march from Falmouth), then the heading 'ADDENDA.', then 'War Department, Quartermaster-General's Office, December 6, 1878' from Meigs to Capt. R. N. Scott (in charge of the War Records publication office) saying the June 1863 Ingalls correspondence was not found, with an inclosure 'August 3, 1863. Abstract of papers relating to horses lost or abandoned on the march of the Army of the Potomac'. The page is Union only: OCR of the running heads shows UNION on every page from p.5 to p.857 and the first 'CONFEDERATE CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.' heading on p.858. So the list's 'Union / Confederate (section transition)' label is wrong, and 'printed chronologically for June 3-August 3, 1863' does not fit the 1878 addenda. Wayback capture 2021-06-19 of the eHistory URL is 'Serial 045 Page 0843 ... UNION' with the same text.
reviews.extraction_notes: Page opens mid-letter (Le Duc's letter begins on p.841, so quote pp.841-843 together). Page footnote reads 'Ingalls to Meigs, August 18, p. 841'; the eHistory capture has 'August 28', a transcription error, so eHistory is not a safe quote source. OCR errors: 'R. hi. -Scott' (R. N. Scott), 'XJ. S. Army'. The 1878 Meigs cover letter is a post-war compiler's exchange, not a wartime dispatch. The historian corpus has one row on this page (or27-3:p0843.1, dated 1863-08-03, no signer): that is the inclosure; the 1878 letter has no row of its own.

reviews.evidence: p. 941: Listed note is correct: Shingler to Capt. [George D.] Wise, Bottom's Bridge, June 27, forwarding a scout's report on steamers up the Pamunkey; Engineer Bureau, June 27, Gilmer to D. H. Hill (negroes for the defensive lines); then a Salt Sulphur Springs, June 27 letter to Lee. Head '... - CONFEDERATE. 941'.
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 947 (page+6). Richmond-area and southwest Virginia business; note verified.

reviews.written: 1863-06-27 (three items dated June 27, 1863; contemporaneous, printed 1889)
issues: Mostly Richmond-front administration; tied to the invasion only through the Jones letter (continues on p.942).
reviews.evidence: Printed p.941 = leaf 947; header viewed: 'Chap. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-CONFEDERATE. 941'. Content: (1) Bottom's Bridge, June 27, 1863, Col. W. P. Shingler to Capt. [George D. Wise], quoting scout Garrett's note on Union moves near Diascund and 'Some six or eight steamers came up the Pamunkey River yesterday'; (2) Engineer Bureau, June 27, J. F. Gilmer to Maj. Gen. D. H. Hill: 'It is not possible for this Bureau to furnish you additional negroes'; (3) Salt Sulphur Springs, June 27, a letter to Lee that continues on p.942 and is signed SAM. JONES (his words there include a diversion 'perhaps into Pennsylvania'). The list's note 'scout reports near Richmond and engineer correspondence, June 27' is correct and merely omits the third item. Wayback capture 2023-04-26 of the eHistory URL shows the same items.
reviews.extraction_notes: The Sam Jones letter is split across pp.941-942 and its signature is on p.942. The historian row for the Shingler dispatch has a garbled addressee ('Captain : I received last night the following dispatch from Mr.'); the bracketed '[George D. Wise:]' is the editor's addition.

reviews.evidence: p. 1029: Listed note is correct: 'Troops in the Department of Richmond, Maj. Gen. Arnold Elzey, C. S. Army, commanding, July 20, 1863' (Wise's Brigade, Cooke's Brigade, Jenkins' Brigade, Godwin's Command). No dispatch on the page.
reviews.extraction_notes: IA OCR leaf 1035 (page+6). Order-of-battle table; not about Gettysburg.

reviews.written: 1863-07-20 (organization table of the Department of Richmond, Maj. Gen. Arnold Elzey); contemporaneous, printed 1889
issues: Not a writing; a troop table of a department far from Gettysburg.
Historian corpus row p1029.1 is a mis-segmented table heading.
reviews.evidence: Printed p.1029 = leaf 1035; header viewed: 'Chap. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-CONFEDERATE. 1029'. Page image viewed: the heading 'Troops in the Department of Richmond, Maj. Gen. Arnold Elzey, C. S. Army, commanding, July 20, 1863.' over a two-column table (Wise's Brigade / Richmond Defenses under Col. T. S. Rhett; Cooke's Brigade / Chaffin's Farm; Jenkins' Brigade / Drewry's Bluff; Godwin's Command). No dispatch on the page. The list's 'Department of Richmond troop roster, July 20' is accurate. Wayback capture 2023-04-25 of the eHistory URL shows the same heading and table.
reviews.extraction_notes: Two-column table: in the OCR the column headings appear in pairs ('Wise's Brigade. Richmond Defenses. Brig. Gen. Henry A. Wise. Col. T. S. Rhett.') before the unit lines, so which units sit under which heading cannot be read from the text; use the page image. Footnote marks (*, dagger, double dagger, section sign) are scattered. The historian corpus counts one dispatch on this page (or27-3:p1029.1, addressee 'Brig. Gen. Henry A. Wise.', place 'C. S. Army, commanding'): it is the table heading, not a dispatch.

reviews.evidence: Printed p.1059 = leaf 1065 (page_numbers.json gives confidence 85 for this leaf); image viewed: header 'Chap. XXXIX.] CORRESPONDENCE, ETC.-CONFEDERATE. 1059'. The table continues the heading on p.1058, 'Organization of the Army of Northern Virginia, commanded by General Robert E. Lee, C. S. Army, July 31, 1863': Hood's division (Robertson's, Law's, Anderson's, Benning's brigades), then 'SECOND ARMY CORPS, Lieut. Gen. Richard S. Ewell', Rodes' division (Rodes', Doles', Ramseur's, Iverson's, Daniel's brigades), ending mid-Daniel's brigade; Early's division starts on p.1060. No dispatch, order or telegram, so the template wording does not fit. This is the end-of-July organization, after the battle. The Wayback capture 2021-06-13 of the eHistory URL is titled 'Serial 045 Page 1059 ... CONFEDERATE'.
reviews.extraction_notes: Layout hazard: the page is a two-column table, and the Archive OCR reads left column then right column, so Law's and Benning's brigades come out after the 'RODES' DIVISION' heading in the text although the image shows them in Hood's division (right column of the Hood block). Any text-based reading will misplace them; read the image. The eHistory transcription of this page omits the printed line '8th Georgia, Col. John R. Towers.' (verified in the scan image and absent from the 2021 capture), so it is not verbatim. 'Iverson's Brigade' is printed with Brig. Gen. S. D. Ramseur as commander (as printed, not an OCR error). The page ends mid-organization (Early's division follows on p.1060).
